quick: IV angiography: 500 mg (5 mL of 10%) rapid IV
Crosses placenta; use only if clearly needed
Excreted in milk; consider interrupting feeds
summary: Fluorescein sodium is a fluorescent diagnostic dye used intravenously for retinal/iris angiography and topically to detect corneal/conjunctival defects and assess tear film and contact-lens fit. The usual adult IV angiography dose is 500 mg (5 mL of 10% or 2-3 mL of 25%) injected rapidly. It transiently turns skin yellow and urine bright yellow-orange. Nausea is common after IV injection; serious risks are rare anaphylaxis and tissue necrosis from extravasation.
indications: Diagnostic fluorescein angiography or angioscopy of the retina and iris vasculature (intravenous)
Detection of corneal epithelial defects, abrasions and foreign bodies (topical)
Applanation tonometry, assessment of tear film break-up time, and fitting of hard contact lenses (topical)
Evaluation of fistulae and patency/seal of ocular wounds (topical)

dosage.d: 500 mg (5 mL of 10% solution, or 2-3 mL of 25% solution) injected rapidly into antecubital vein
7.7 mg/kg (0.077 mL/kg of 10% solution), max 500 mg
Moisten sterile strip with sterile saline; touch to bulbar conjunctiva/fornix
dosage.n: Patient blinks to distribute; examine with cobalt blue light
Avoid contaminating dropper; remove soft contact lenses

admin: For IV use, inject rapidly into the antecubital vein after taking care to avoid extravasation
Have epinephrine, antihistamines, oxygen and resuscitation equipment immediately available
Avoid extravasation - the high pH solution can cause severe local tissue damage and sloughing
For topical use, apply a moistened strip or drops to the conjunctival sac and have the patient blink
Remove soft contact lenses before topical use as they absorb and retain the dye
moa: Fluorescein is an inert xanthene dye that absorbs blue light (~465-490 nm) and emits green fluorescence (~520-530 nm). It is not metabolically active; its diagnostic value comes from outlining blood flow when injected intravenously and from pooling in areas of epithelial loss when applied topically, made visible under cobalt-blue illumination.

relative: History of allergy, asthma or prior reaction to fluorescein
Concurrent beta-blocker use (may worsen anaphylaxis management)
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis during and after injection

preg: Fluorescein crosses the placenta after IV administration. Adequate human data are lacking; use intravenous fluorescein during pregnancy only if the diagnostic benefit clearly justifies the potential risk. Topical use carries minimal systemic exposure.
lact: Fluorescein is excreted into breast milk for up to several days after IV injection. Consider interrupting breastfeeding (and discarding milk) for about 24-72 hours after intravenous angiography; topical use poses minimal risk.
renal: Fluorescein is eliminated mainly by renal excretion (with some hepatic metabolism to glucuronide); use caution in renal impairment as clearance is reduced and skin/urine discoloration may persist longer.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established for hepatic impairment; fluorescein is partly conjugated in the liver.

moderate: Beta-blockers - may blunt response to epinephrine if anaphylaxis occurs
minor: Concurrent IV medications - flush line; fluorescein may interfere with some assays
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: Causes transient interference with clinical laboratory tests for up to ~3-4 days (e.g., fluorometric assays, some serum/urine analyses); markedly discolors urine yellow-orange.

common: Nausea (often transient, after rapid IV injection)
Transient yellowing of skin and sclera

monitoring: Close observation for hypersensitivity during and for a period after IV injection
Injection site for signs of extravasation
Vital signs in patients with cardiac or allergic history
Resuscitation readiness before each IV administration
counsel: Your skin may look slightly yellow and your urine bright orange for a day or so - this is normal
Tell the staff immediately if you feel itchy, short of breath, dizzy or have throat tightness
Some nausea right after the injection is common and passes quickly
Remove soft contact lenses before eye-drop staining; they can be stained
Drink fluids to help clear the dye after angiography
pk: Retinal fluorescence within ~10-15 seconds of IV injection
Skin/urine discoloration fades over 24-36 hours; cleared in ~24-72 h
Store at 20-25 C; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Always have anaphylaxis treatment (epinephrine, oxygen) ready before IV fluorescein angiography
Extravasation is painful and can cause tissue necrosis - inject carefully and stop if pain occurs
Warn patients about transient yellow skin and bright orange urine to avoid alarm
Can interfere with laboratory and fluorometric assays for several days
Remove soft contact lenses before topical staining; viewed best under cobalt-blue light
missed: Not applicable - fluorescein is a single-use diagnostic agent administered by clinical staff for a specific examination, not a scheduled self-administered medication.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely with standard diagnostic doses. Excessive IV exposure may intensify nausea, vomiting and hypersensitivity reactions. Management is supportive, with treatment of allergic/anaphylactic reactions (epinephrine, antihistamines, airway support) and hydration to promote renal clearance.
